Mr. Chairman, I think most members of the house like myself who have not had legal training must feel a little confused with all the legal explanations that have been coming from both sides of the house during the last day and a half. I feel something like the coloured gentleman who was arrested for stealing chickens. There seemed to be a pretty definite case against him. A friend of his met him on the street a few days after when he thought he should be in jail, and he said, "Rastus, didn't you steal them chickens?" Rastus said, "I thought I did until I heard my lawyer talk to the judge." That is about how I feel in connection with this Emergency Powers Act.
I think we have had some clarification in the last few minutes, and now some of us understand it better than we did before. We realize that what we are doing here is giving the government powers equal to those of parliament, with the few exceptions that have been mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition and others-very minor exceptions I would say. Those powers may be exercised when parliament is in session as well as when parliament is not in session.
Why should we give the governor in council the power to do things that would ordinarily be done by parliament when it is in session? The Emergency Powers Act would be more sensible and logical if it provided that the government should only exercise these powers when parliament was not in session. Then when parliament was called the powers given to the government by the Emergency Powers Act would lapse and parliament would again become supreme. Then it seems to me the government would be on much stronger ground in asking for powers of that kind. There would be much greater certainty.
I do not profess to have all the fears that members of the official opposition have that the government may misuse its powers. Of course there is always the danger that a 68108-1161
Emergency Powers Act government may misuse its powers; but fortunately, as things are now, if members of the official opposition were on the other side of the house and the members of the government were on this side I do not think I would have any greater fears that they would misuse their powers.
But there is always that danger that a government may do so, and the more a government becomes accustomed to having powers without continual control by parliament the more the danger is increased. There may be no merit at all in what I have said; nevertheless I think it would be much better if the government had the right to exercise such powers, in times that are somewhat critical, when parliament is not in session and then when parliament convened the Emergency Powers Act would lapse until such time as parliament was again not in session.

In reply to my hon. friend's questions, may I say that the orders in council that have been passed themselves indicate that no facts have arisen during the past two years which would make the possession of the powers covered by this statute absolutely essential. But I thought -I had rather made clear, indeed had laboured the point on two or three occasions previously, that the nature of emergency powers is this. Where a government is in the emergency of apprehended war or the emergency of the changeover from war to peace, which was the basis of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, the necessity for the executive government having these powers arises from the fact that unforeseen need for their use can arise. The mere fact that need has not arisen during the preceding year or two years is no guarantee at all that it may not arise two days from now, two weeks from now or a month from now.
Let me take a concrete example. Within the next year and a half-I think before August, 1954-we have to have a general election in Canada. Having regard to the

Emergency Powers Act state of the world at the present time, if during the time parliament was completely out of existence because of dissolution-and no new parliament can meet until the general election is held-

-in Asia or in any other place which required, perhaps in a matter of hours, urgent action upon the part of the country, that action can only be taken by the government if it possesses the type of emergency powers which are covered by this statute.
Perhaps I might point to another practical instance of this sort of thing, the War Measures Act itself, which was put on the statute books in 1914 at the time of world war I and has been permitted to remain there ever since, even during times of peace, in order to provide for wartime emergencies when they arise. As I have pointed out before, the real significance of the present statute is that it provides a method by which emergency powers which it is prudent to have in times of apprehended war, and which otherwise would be available in any case under the War Measures Act, may be exercised in such a manner as to provide parliament with a proper measure of control over actions taken by the government pursuant to those powers.
The Leader of the Opposition says-and I think this statement is also repeated by some of his followers-that the necessity of prompt tabling of these orders in council within a matter of five days, and the power which is given under the Emergency Powers Act to any member of parliament, any member of the opposition, to put a resolution upon the order paper seeking annulment of any order in council passed by the government which he thinks is an abuse or improper use of its powers, is of no practical significance. Why? Because he says we all know that since the opposition is a minority in parliament it will not be able to get the resolution passed and in that way will not be able to challenge successfully the action which the government has taken in the particular order in council.
But surely if the same process of reasoning is applied to a bill which the government brings into parliament, rather than handling the matter by order in council, then when this bill commands the support of the government


majority, every member of the opposition is in substantially the same position of disability in relation to that bill as he is in relation to the resolution by which he seeks annulment of a government order in council. That disability is, I suggest, inherent and unavoidable in our system of democratic government which provides that when we have had an election and the will of the people has become known, the government is formed by the majority in parliament. Of course when it is formed by the majority it cannot remain a government unless it retains control of the majority of the members. As long as it has that control it is in the nature of things that when it introduces a piece of legislation it will be able to get it passed or cease to be a government. By the very same process in reverse it is in the nature of things that when an order in council passed by the government under its emergency powers is attacked by annulment proceedings then, as the Leader of the Opposition rightly says, the likelihood is that the application for annulment will not be successful.
